Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question:
A nightly reporting job must scan a large Amazon DynamoDB table to generate a usage summary, and the scan needs to finish faster without disrupting live traffic. Ivywood Networks, a video conferencing SaaS company that runs this job during off-peak hours, currently sees production traffic consume around 50% of the table's provisioned read capacity even during the scan window.
Which two actions should a developer take to minimize the time required to produce the report without affecting production workloads? (Select TWO.)
Correct Answer(s):
Use the Limit parameter

Use a Parallel Scan API operation
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer):
Keyword tip: look for phrases like "throttling protection" or "rate-limiting during a scan" as signals to use the Limit parameter together with parallel scan segments.

Keyword tip: phrases like "divide into segments" and "multiple workers scanning concurrently" point to Parallel Scan.
Your Answer(s):
Use a Sequential Scan API operation

Increase read capacity units during the scan operation
Overall Explanation:
This question tests the ability to optimize a DynamoDB Scan operation so that it finishes faster while protecting the provisioned throughput that production traffic needs. A sequential scan reads one segment at a time and is limited by the throughput of that single segment, so it is only appropriate for small tables or when speed is not a priority. A parallel scan divides the table into multiple segments and lets multiple workers scan those segments at the same time, which is the correct approach when the goal is to finish a scan on a large table quickly. The Limit parameter caps how many items each worker request returns, which prevents any single worker from consuming all of the throughput and starving the other workers or the production workload. The correct combination is parallel scan for speed and the Limit parameter for throughput control, while increasing capacity or relying on default pagination does not solve the actual constraint in this scenario.
Consider this scenario: Ivywood Networks runs a nightly usage report against a DynamoDB table that stores video conferencing session metadata for thousands of active meetings. Running a single sequential scan during business hours would compete with live meeting traffic for the same read capacity, causing latency for users joining or managing calls. By switching to a parallel scan with a bounded Limit parameter per worker, the engineering team finishes the report in a fraction of the time while keeping enough throughput available for production API calls.
References:
https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/developer/rate-limited-scans-in-amazon-dynamodb/
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Scan.html#Scan.ParallelScan

https://cloudforall.com.br/cursos/aws-developer-associate-dva-c02-english/flashcards/
Option 1: Use the Limit parameter
Option 1 Explanation: Correct. The Limit parameter sets the maximum number of items that a single Scan request returns. This setting stops one worker in a parallel scan from consuming all of the table's available read capacity. The Limit parameter protects the other workers and the production traffic from being starved of throughput. Keyword tip: look for phrases like "throttling protection" or "rate-limiting during a scan" as signals to use the Limit parameter together with parallel scan segments.
Option 2: Use a Sequential Scan API operation
Option 2 Explanation: Incorrect. A sequential scan processes the table one segment at a time. A sequential scan is limited by the throughput available to that single segment, so the scan takes longer to finish. This behavior directly conflicts with the goal of minimizing scan time. Keyword tip: "Sequential Scan" describes the default, slower behavior and is rarely the correct choice when the goal is to minimize scan duration.
Option 3: Increase read capacity units during the scan operation
Option 3 Explanation: Incorrect. Increasing read capacity units would make the scan run faster, but it raises cost. Increasing read capacity units does not address the requirement to use the existing provisioned throughput efficiently without affecting production traffic. Keyword tip: treat any option that adds more provisioned capacity to fix a performance problem as a cost-inefficient shortcut, not the best-practice answer.
Option 4: Use a Parallel Scan API operation
Option 4 Explanation: Correct. The Parallel Scan API operation divides the table or index into multiple logical segments. Multiple workers scan different segments at the same time, which overcomes the throughput limit of scanning one segment sequentially. This approach significantly reduces the total time needed to complete the scan. Keyword tip: phrases like "divide into segments" and "multiple workers scanning concurrently" point to Parallel Scan.
Option 5: Use pagination to divide results into pages sized at DynamoDB's default per-request data limit
Option 5 Explanation: Incorrect. Pagination is simply how DynamoDB returns Scan results by default, dividing output into fixed-size response pages. Pagination does not distribute the scan workload across partitions and does not limit throughput consumption per worker, so it does not help minimize scan time or protect production throughput. Keyword tip: pagination controls how results are retrieved, not how work is parallelized or throttled.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question:
Eastwick Systems needs to roll out a new feature to a small group of beta testers without affecting the experience of its existing users, as part of a serverless application it operates for a public university with a large, active student body. The new feature involves an AWS Lambda function that is invoked by an Amazon API Gateway API, and the API currently uses a specific Lambda alias to invoke the function.
What would be the most efficient approach to meet these requirements?
Correct Answer(s): Create a new version of the Lambda function. Build a new stage on API Gateway integrated with this new Lambda version. Utilize this new API Gateway stage for beta testing.
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: a dedicated API Gateway stage mapped to a new Lambda version is the standard pattern for isolated beta testing.
Your Answer(s): Use AWS CodeDeploy to deploy the updated Lambda function. Split traffic between the new and old versions of the function for testing purposes.
Overall Explanation:
This question tests knowledge of AWS Lambda versions and aliases combined with Amazon API Gateway stages as a way to isolate a small group of users for testing. A Lambda version is an immutable snapshot of function code. An API Gateway stage can point to a specific Lambda version or alias, so you can create a separate stage for beta testers while the production stage keeps serving existing users unchanged. AWS CodeDeploy shifts a percentage of traffic between Lambda versions during a deployment, which is useful for gradual, population-wide rollouts, but it cannot target a specific, known group of users. The correct choice depends on whether the requirement is precise audience isolation, which favors a dedicated stage, or gradual rollout to an unknown population, which favors CodeDeploy traffic shifting.
Real-world example: Eastwick Systems, a public university, could use this pattern to test a new course-registration feature with a small group of faculty advisors before releasing it to the entire student body. The advisors would use a separate API Gateway stage that points to the new Lambda version, while students continue using the stable production stage. This setup keeps the beta test isolated and prevents any disruption to the live registration system during peak enrollment periods.
References:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/set-up-stages.html
Flashcards (free, no signup required, by domain):

Option 1: Create a new version of the Lambda function. Build a new stage on API Gateway integrated with this new Lambda version. Utilize this new API Gateway stage for beta testing.
Option 1 Explanation: Correct. Publishing a new Lambda version creates an immutable snapshot of the function code. Creating a new API Gateway stage that points to this new Lambda version gives beta testers a separate endpoint to call. Existing users keep using the original stage and alias, so their experience does not change. Keyword tip: a dedicated API Gateway stage mapped to a new Lambda version is the standard pattern for isolated beta testing.
Option 2: Use the AWS CLI to manually switch between the old and new versions of the Lambda function during testing periods.
Option 2 Explanation: Incorrect. Manually switching between Lambda versions with the AWS CLI requires a person to perform the switch every time. This approach is slow and prone to human error. It also does not separate beta testers from existing users, because everyone still calls the same Lambda alias. Keyword tip: manual CLI switching for production traffic control is a sign of an inefficient, unmanaged approach.
Option 3: Use AWS CodeDeploy to deploy the updated Lambda function. Split traffic between the new and old versions of the function for testing purposes.
Option 3 Explanation: Incorrect. AWS CodeDeploy can shift a percentage of traffic from one Lambda version to another. This capability is useful for canary or linear deployments that reduce risk during a production rollout. AWS CodeDeploy does not let you target a specific, known group of beta users; it only shifts a random percentage of all traffic. Keyword tip: CodeDeploy traffic shifting supports gradual production rollout, not isolation of a defined beta group.
Option 4: Implement Amazon S3 bucket versioning on the Lambda function code. For testing purposes, link the API Gateway to the new version of the code stored in the S3 bucket.
Option 4 Explanation: Incorrect. Amazon S3 bucket versioning tracks different versions of objects stored in a bucket. API Gateway cannot invoke a Lambda function directly from a specific S3 object version. This option confuses S3 object versioning with Lambda function versioning, which are separate and unrelated features. Keyword tip: S3 versioning applies to stored objects, not to Lambda function versions or API Gateway routing.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question:
Eastwick Agency, a music streaming platform headquartered in Austin, Texas, is building a new listener-facing application that must support Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) authentication as well as sign-in through social identity providers such as Google or Facebook. The application also needs authorization to directly access listener data stored in Amazon S3 buckets and Amazon DynamoDB tables.
Which AWS service or feature will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of additional coding?
Correct Answer(s): Amazon Cognito identity pools
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: when a scenario needs AWS resource access after SAML, social, or federated sign-in, Amazon Cognito identity pools is the correct choice.
Your Answer(s): Amazon Cognito user pools
Overall Explanation:
This question tests the difference between Amazon Cognito user pools and Amazon Cognito identity pools. Amazon Cognito user pools act as a user directory and handle authentication, including sign-in through SAML and through social identity providers. Amazon Cognito identity pools handle authorization: an identity pool takes an already-authenticated identity and exchanges it for temporary, limited-privilege AWS credentials through AWS STS. Use identity pools whenever an application needs direct, scoped access to AWS services such as Amazon S3 or DynamoDB after a user signs in through SAML, social, or other federated identity providers, because identity pools support many identity provider types natively and require minimal custom code.
A similar situation: Eastwick Agency wants listeners to sign in with their existing Google account or through their record label's SAML-based single sign-on, then have the mobile application read and write playlist data stored in DynamoDB and stream album art stored in S3. By placing an Amazon Cognito identity pool behind the sign-in flow, Eastwick Agency avoids building a custom authorization server and instead lets AWS STS issue temporary credentials scoped to exactly the S3 and DynamoDB resources each listener is allowed to use.
References:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html
https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/knowledge-center/cognito-user-pools-identity-pools/
Flashcards (free, no signup required, by domain):
https://cloudforall.com.br/cursos/aws-developer-associate-dva-c02-english/flashcards/
Option 1: Amazon API Gateway REST API
Option 1 Explanation: Incorrect. Amazon API Gateway REST API is used to expose and manage APIs. Amazon API Gateway does not authenticate users against SAML or social identity providers, and it does not issue AWS credentials on its own. Building a custom REST API layer to bridge authentication and AWS access would require significantly more coding than a managed federation service. Keyword tip: Amazon API Gateway handles API routing, throttling, and management, not identity federation or credential vending.
Option 2: AWS AppSync GraphQL API
Option 2 Explanation: Incorrect. AWS AppSync provides a managed GraphQL API layer for querying and updating data. AWS AppSync does not solve an authentication-and-authorization problem by itself. Adding AWS AppSync here would introduce unnecessary development work instead of reducing it. Keyword tip: AWS AppSync is for building GraphQL APIs with resolvers and real-time data sync, not for issuing AWS credentials to authenticated users.
Option 3: Amazon Cognito user pools
Option 3 Explanation: Incorrect. Amazon Cognito user pools handle user authentication. A user pool can accept sign-in through SAML and through social identity providers. A user pool does not give an application temporary AWS credentials. To reach Amazon S3 or DynamoDB, Eastwick Agency would still need to pair the user pool with an identity pool. This pairing adds extra coding, so this option does not meet the LEAST-coding requirement. Keyword tip: user pools handle authentication and sign-up/sign-in; identity pools handle authorization and AWS credentials.
Option 4: Amazon Cognito identity pools
Option 4 Explanation: Correct. Amazon Cognito identity pools, also called federated identities, accept identities from SAML providers, social identity providers, OpenID Connect providers, Amazon Cognito user pools, or developer-authenticated identities. An identity pool exchanges these identities for temporary, limited-privilege AWS credentials through AWS STS. Eastwick Agency's application can use these credentials to access Amazon S3 and DynamoDB directly, without writing custom authorization logic. Keyword tip: when a scenario needs AWS resource access after SAML, social, or federated sign-in, Amazon Cognito identity pools is the correct choice.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question:
Truenorth Dynamics, a biotechnology research lab, operates a genomic sequencing pipeline on Amazon EC2 that produces a high volume of small metadata files, each about 1 KB in size, containing personally identifiable information about research subjects that must be converted to ciphertext. The lab stores these files on an in-house, proprietary network-attached storage appliance that has no native integration with AWS KMS.
What is the SAFEST way to encrypt the data using AWS KMS?
Correct Answer(s): Encrypt the data directly with a customer managed customer master key
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: when payload size is at or below 4 KB and the scenario requires full customer control over the key, encrypt the data directly with a customer managed customer master key.
Your Answer(s): Create a data encryption key from a customer master key and encrypt the data with the data encryption key
Overall Explanation:
AWS KMS supports two main encryption approaches: direct encryption with a customer master key, and envelope encryption with a data encryption key. Direct encryption works only for payloads up to 4 KB per operation, but it keeps the key material inside AWS KMS at all times, making it the safest option for small files. Envelope encryption is required for larger data volumes, but it forces the customer to manage the data encryption key's lifecycle outside of AWS KMS, which adds operational risk. The choice between an AWS managed customer master key and a customer managed customer master key depends on who needs control: AWS managed keys only exist for specific AWS service integrations, while customer managed keys give the customer full control and work with any storage system, including non-AWS systems.
Real-world example: A biotechnology research lab like Truenorth Dynamics generates thousands of small metadata files during genomic sequencing runs, each containing personally identifiable information about research participants. Because these files are stored on an in-house network-attached storage appliance with no native AWS integration, the lab cannot rely on an AWS managed customer master key. Encrypting each file directly with a customer managed customer master key lets the lab's security team retain full control over key policies and rotation while meeting strict data privacy requirements for research subject data.
References:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/concepts.html
Flashcards (free, no signup required, by domain):
https://cloudforall.com.br/cursos/aws-developer-associate-dva-c02-english/flashcards/
Option 1: Encrypt the data directly with a customer managed customer master key
Option 1 Explanation: Correct. A customer managed customer master key is created and fully controlled by the customer, including its key policy, IAM permissions, grants, rotation schedule, and deletion timeline. Each file is only 1 KB, which is within the 4 KB limit for direct encryption through the KMS Encrypt API, so no data encryption key is needed. Because the key material of a customer managed customer master key never leaves AWS KMS, this method gives the strongest security guarantee with the least operational complexity for small files. Keyword tip: when payload size is at or below 4 KB and the scenario requires full customer control over the key, encrypt the data directly with a customer managed customer master key.
Option 2: Create a data encryption key from a customer master key and encrypt the data with the customer master key
Option 2 Explanation: Incorrect. This option creates a data encryption key from a customer master key, but then encrypts the file with the customer master key instead of the data encryption key. Creating the data encryption key serves no purpose in this workflow, because the file is never encrypted with it. This wastes an extra API call to AWS KMS without adding any security benefit. Keyword tip: watch for options where a data encryption key is generated but the actual encryption step still uses the customer master key directly; this signals a broken envelope encryption workflow.
Option 3: Create a data encryption key from a customer master key and encrypt the data with the data encryption key
Option 3 Explanation: Incorrect. Creating a data encryption key from a customer master key and using the data encryption key to encrypt the data is the standard envelope encryption pattern. This pattern is designed for large files or high-volume encryption, because a customer master key can only encrypt up to 4 KB of data directly. Each file in this scenario is only 1 KB, so it fits within the direct encryption limit, and adding a separately managed data encryption key only increases operational risk without any benefit. Keyword tip: choose envelope encryption with a data encryption key only when data exceeds 4 KB or when the workload has high-volume or high-performance encryption needs.
Option 4: Encrypt the data directly with an AWS managed customer master key
Option 4 Explanation: Incorrect. An AWS managed customer master key is created and controlled by an AWS service, such as Amazon S3 or Amazon EBS, when that service needs to encrypt data on the customer's behalf. Truenorth Dynamics stores its files on a proprietary, non-AWS network-attached storage system, so no AWS service exists to request or manage an AWS managed customer master key for this data. Keyword tip: an AWS managed customer master key only appears when a supported AWS service creates it automatically; proprietary or unsupported storage systems cannot use one.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question:
Larkspur Robotics needs to let users sign in to its new web application from any source, while automatically blocking any sign-in attempt that is flagged as high risk. The company, which supplies robotics kits and curriculum to K-12 school districts, uses Amazon Cognito to handle authentication for this application.
Which Amazon Cognito feature will meet these requirements?
Correct Answer(s): Adaptive authentication
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: when a scenario describes automatically blocking or challenging sign-ins based on a calculated risk level, adaptive authentication is the feature being tested.
Your Answer(s): Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
Overall Explanation:
This question tests the difference between three Amazon Cognito capabilities: a static authentication factor (MFA), passive risk reporting (advanced security metrics), and automated risk-based response (adaptive authentication). Adaptive authentication is the correct choice whenever a requirement calls for dynamically allowing, challenging, or blocking sign-in attempts based on a calculated risk score. Advanced security metrics only send risk data to CloudWatch for visibility; the metrics do not take action on their own. MFA only adds a fixed second-factor step and does not respond to risk level at all. The key decision logic is to identify whether the requirement needs automated risk-driven action, passive reporting, or a fixed authentication step, and match that need to adaptive authentication, advanced security metrics, or MFA respectively.
Practical example: A K-12 software vendor like Larkspur Robotics lets students, teachers, and parents sign in to a shared portal from many different networks and devices, including school computers, home computers, and personal phones. To keep the portal open to legitimate users everywhere while still protecting student data, Larkspur Robotics configures adaptive authentication so that Amazon Cognito automatically blocks any sign-in attempt that scores as high risk, without requiring the company to build custom risk-detection logic.
References:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-user-pool-settings-adaptive-authentication.html
Flashcards (free, no signup required, by domain):
https://cloudforall.com.br/cursos/aws-developer-associate-dva-c02-english/flashcards/
Option 1: Advanced security metrics
Option 1 Explanation: Incorrect. Advanced security metrics send sign-in attempt data, risk levels, and failed challenge information to Amazon CloudWatch. This data supports monitoring and analysis. Advanced security metrics do not take any automated action to block a sign-in. Keyword tip: treat metrics as an observability tool, not an enforcement tool. Enforcement requires adaptive authentication.
Option 2: Case-sensitive user pools
Option 2 Explanation: Incorrect. Case-sensitive user pools control whether Amazon Cognito treats letter case as significant in usernames and email addresses during sign-in. This setting has no connection to threat detection or risk-based responses. Keyword tip: link this feature only to username and email string matching, never to risk evaluation or security enforcement.
Option 3: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
Option 3 Explanation: Incorrect. MFA makes users provide a second authentication factor. MFA does not evaluate risk. MFA does not block a sign-in attempt automatically based on risk level. To block sign-ins automatically based on risk, Larkspur Robotics must configure adaptive authentication with a Block response for the target risk level. Keyword tip: MFA only adds a challenge step. MFA does not calculate or react to a risk score.
Option 4: Adaptive authentication
Option 4 Explanation: Correct. Adaptive authentication evaluates each sign-in attempt and assigns a risk score. The risk score is based on signals such as a new device, an unusual location, or a suspicious IP address. Larkspur Robotics can configure a response for each risk level, including Allow, Optional MFA, Require MFA, or Block. This lets the company automatically block sign-in attempts at an elevated risk level. Keyword tip: when a scenario describes automatically blocking or challenging sign-ins based on a calculated risk level, adaptive authentication is the feature being tested.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question:
A recent internal audit found that a flagship crop-yield prediction application was often deployed with outdated code, because engineers had to manually trigger the deployment pipeline after each source code change and sometimes forgot to do so. Yellowpine Solutions, the agricultural technology company that owns the application, wants to build and deploy the application automatically as soon as any change is made to the source code.
As a Developer Associate, which of the following options would you suggest to trigger the deployment? (Select TWO.)
Correct Answer(s):
Keep the source code in an Amazon S3 bucket and start AWS CodePipeline whenever a file in the S3 bucket is updated

Keep the source code in an AWS CodeCommit repository and start AWS CodePipeline whenever a change is pushed to the CodeCommit repository
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer):
Keyword tip: S3 combined with an event-driven trigger through EventBridge is the recommended change-detection method for CodePipeline.

Keyword tip: a CodeCommit push event triggering CodePipeline through EventBridge is the standard pattern for source-code-driven CI/CD.
Your Answer(s):
Keep the source code in an AWS CodeCommit repository and start AWS CodePipeline whenever a change is pushed to the CodeCommit repository

Keep the source code in Amazon EFS and start AWS CodePipeline whenever a file is updated
Overall Explanation:
This question tests knowledge of which source providers AWS CodePipeline supports and how a pipeline can start automatically after a source code change. AWS CodePipeline natively supports Amazon S3 and AWS CodeCommit, as well as certain third-party providers like GitHub, as source stages. The recommended change-detection method for these sources is an Amazon EventBridge rule that starts the pipeline immediately when a change happens, instead of relying on periodic polling, which adds delay. Amazon EFS and Amazon EBS are not valid CodePipeline source providers, because they are file and block storage services without a built-in pipeline-trigger integration, so they cannot be used to detect source code changes automatically.
Real-world example: An agricultural technology company like Yellowpine Solutions relies on frequent, timely updates to its crop-yield prediction models to support farmers during planting and harvest seasons. By storing the application source code in AWS CodeCommit and letting an Amazon EventBridge rule start AWS CodePipeline on every push, the engineering team removes the manual trigger step that previously caused outdated deployments, and new model improvements reach production automatically and without delay.
References:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/pipelines-about-starting.html
Flashcards (free, no signup required, by domain):
https://cloudforall.com.br/cursos/aws-developer-associate-dva-c02-english/flashcards/
Option 1: Keep the source code in an Amazon EBS volume and start AWS CodePipeline whenever there are updates to the source code
Option 1 Explanation: Incorrect. Amazon EBS is block storage attached to a single EC2 instance. Amazon EBS is not a supported or practical source provider for AWS CodePipeline, and there is no built-in change-detection integration between EBS and CodePipeline. Keyword tip: EBS is instance-attached block storage, not a pipeline source repository, so it should never be chosen as a CodePipeline trigger mechanism.
Option 2: Keep the source code in an Amazon S3 bucket and start AWS CodePipeline whenever a file in the S3 bucket is updated
Option 2 Explanation: Correct. Amazon S3 is a supported source provider for AWS CodePipeline. When a pipeline uses an S3 bucket as its source, CodePipeline automatically creates an Amazon EventBridge rule. This rule starts the pipeline as soon as an object in the bucket changes. This gives Yellowpine Solutions a near real-time, event-driven deployment process instead of a manual one. Keyword tip: S3 combined with an event-driven trigger through EventBridge is the recommended change-detection method for CodePipeline.
Option 3: Keep the source code in an AWS CodeCommit repository and start AWS CodePipeline whenever a change is pushed to the CodeCommit repository
Option 3 Explanation: Correct. AWS CodeCommit is a fully supported source provider for AWS CodePipeline. When a pipeline uses a CodeCommit repository as its source, CodePipeline automatically creates an Amazon EventBridge rule. This rule starts the pipeline as soon as a change is pushed to the repository, giving Yellowpine Solutions an automatic, event-driven build and deployment process. Keyword tip: a CodeCommit push event triggering CodePipeline through EventBridge is the standard pattern for source-code-driven CI/CD.
Option 4: Keep the source code in an Amazon S3 bucket and set up AWS CodePipeline to recur at an interval of every 15 minutes
Option 4 Explanation: Incorrect. Polling an S3 bucket at a fixed interval, such as every 15 minutes, is an older change-detection method. This method adds delay compared to event-driven triggers, and AWS recommends disabling periodic checks in favor of an EventBridge rule. Keyword tip: a fixed polling interval, like 15 minutes, is a signal of an inefficient, non-recommended trigger method.
Option 5: Keep the source code in Amazon EFS and start AWS CodePipeline whenever a file is updated
Option 5 Explanation: Incorrect. Amazon EFS is not a supported source provider for AWS CodePipeline. There is no built-in mechanism that lets CodePipeline detect changes to files stored in an EFS file system. Keyword tip: only Amazon S3, AWS CodeCommit, and certain supported third-party repositories, such as GitHub, can act as CodePipeline source stages.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question:
Novapoint Technologies, a mining and minerals company, operates a fleet of automated ore-sorting machines across its extraction sites. The company uses an AWS Lambda function to run real-time image-analysis algorithms that classify mineral samples from sensor data, and this function is highly CPU-intensive due to the complexity of the image-processing calculations.
The engineering team now needs to reduce the average runtime of this function without rewriting its underlying code.
Which of the following approaches should be recommended to achieve this goal?
Correct Answer(s): Deploy the function with its memory allocation set to the maximum amount
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: for compute-heavy Lambda functions, increasing the memory setting is the primary way to increase effective CPU performance.
Your Answer(s): Deploy the function using Lambda layers
Overall Explanation:
This question tests understanding of how AWS Lambda allocates compute resources to a function. Lambda does not let a developer set CPU power directly. Lambda scales CPU power automatically and proportionally based on the memory setting configured for the function. A developer should increase the memory setting when a function is CPU-intensive and the runtime needs to decrease. A developer should use Lambda layers to share code or libraries across functions, not to improve performance. A developer should use multi-Region deployment to reduce latency for distributed users or to support disaster recovery, not to speed up a single function invocation. The core decision logic is recognizing that in the Lambda execution model, memory and CPU power are linked, so increasing memory is the actual lever for improving compute performance.
Use case: Novapoint Technologies runs an image-analysis function that classifies mineral samples from sensor data at its mining sites, and this function performs heavy computational work on each invocation. By increasing the memory allocation of this function, Novapoint Technologies increases the available CPU capacity for each invocation, which reduces the average processing time for each sample without requiring any changes to the function's code. This approach lets the company process ore-sorting data faster and keep pace with the throughput of its automated sorting machines.
References:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-memory.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-layers.html
Flashcards (free, no signup required, by domain):
https://cloudforall.com.br/cursos/aws-developer-associate-dva-c02-english/flashcards/
Option 1: Deploy the function with its memory allocation set to the maximum amount
Option 1 Explanation: Correct. Lambda allocates CPU power in proportion to the memory configured for a function. Increasing the memory setting proportionally increases the vCPU capacity available to the function. Lambda memory can scale up to 10 GB, which is the maximum configurable amount. This higher CPU capacity reduces runtime for CPU-intensive workloads, such as image-processing calculations. Keyword tip: for compute-heavy Lambda functions, increasing the memory setting is the primary way to increase effective CPU performance.
Option 2: Deploy the function using Lambda layers
Option 2 Explanation: Incorrect. Lambda layers are .zip archives that let a developer share code, custom runtimes, libraries, or configuration files across multiple functions. Layers help with code reuse and separation of concerns. Layers do not change the amount of CPU or memory allocated to a function's execution environment. Keyword tip: layers solve code organization and reuse problems, not performance or runtime problems.
Option 3: Deploy the function with its CPU allocation set to the maximum amount
Option 3 Explanation: Incorrect. AWS Lambda does not provide a setting that lets a developer configure CPU power directly. Lambda allocates CPU power automatically. Lambda calculates this allocation based on the memory setting of the function. A developer cannot configure CPU power as an independent setting. Keyword tip: if an option claims a Lambda function lets you set CPU directly, treat that option as invalid, because Lambda always ties compute power to the memory setting.
Option 4: Deploy the function into multiple AWS Regions
Option 4 Explanation: Incorrect. Deploying a Lambda function into multiple AWS Regions places copies of the function closer to end users in different geographic locations. This deployment pattern reduces latency and improves resilience. This deployment pattern does not change the compute capacity or CPU performance available to any single function invocation. Keyword tip: multi-Region deployment is a resilience and latency strategy, not a compute optimization technique.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question:
A recent internal audit at an education technology company flagged a compliance risk: automated logs generated by a serverless grading platform might unintentionally capture student personal information. The audit was triggered after a data-privacy review of Orchardvale Systems' AWS Lambda-based assignment-scoring service, which streams runtime diagnostics to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
Orchardvale Systems needs a way to guarantee that no personally identifiable information (PII) about students ends up persisted within those log streams.
What strategy should the developer adopt to meet this requirement?
Correct Answer(s): Configure Amazon CloudWatch Logs data protection to detect and mask PII in log events (using managed data identifiers) before the data is stored.
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: the phrase "data protection policy" together with "managed data identifiers" in CloudWatch Logs points to this native detect-and-mask capability.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question:
A recent internal security audit flagged an application running on Amazon ECS for using long-lived access keys, originally set up for development testing, to call Amazon DynamoDB through the AWS SDK. The audit findings triggered an urgent fix before the application moves to a production cluster.
Keystone Collective, an e-learning platform that hosts video coursework and stores student progress data, now needs to close this gap before deployment continues.
How should the developer configure the application to securely authenticate to AWS services?
Correct Answer(s): Configure an ECS task IAM role for the application to use.
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: "task IAM role" is the standard secure-authentication pattern for ECS tasks calling AWS services like DynamoDB.
Your Answer(s): Configure the credentials file with a new access key/secret access key.
Overall Explanation:
This question tests secure credential management for containerized workloads on Amazon ECS. The correct pattern is an ECS task IAM role, which attaches directly to the task definition and provides temporary, automatically rotated credentials scoped only to that task's containers. An ECS instance profile works differently: it grants permissions to the EC2 instance itself, so every task running on that instance shares the same permissions, which breaks the principle of least privilege. Static access keys, whether stored in environment variables or in a credentials file, are long-lived credentials that require manual rotation and increase the risk of exposure.
Consider this scenario: Keystone Collective's engineering team is migrating an ECS-based grading service that calls DynamoDB to store student progress data. Instead of packaging developer access keys into the container image, the team defines an ECS task IAM role scoped to only the DynamoDB tables the grading service needs. This way, if one microservice is compromised, the blast radius stays limited to that specific task's permissions, and CloudTrail logs show exactly which task made each API call.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question:
Bluecrest Alliance, a state government agency, runs an application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances that manages citizen benefit records. The application uses the AWS SDK for Java to copy files into several Amazon S3 buckets, using access keys stored in environment variables. A developer at Bluecrest Alliance has modified the instances to use an assumed IAM role with a more restrictive policy that allows access to only one bucket.
However, after applying the change, the developer logs into one of the instances and finds that the application is still able to write to all buckets.
What is the MOST likely explanation for this situation?
Correct Answer(s): The AWS credential provider looks for instance profile credentials last
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: when environment variables and an instance role are both present, the credential chain always uses the environment variables first.
Your Answer(s): An IAM managed policy is being used on the IAM role
Overall Explanation:
The AWS SDK for Java resolves credentials through a default provider chain with a fixed search order: environment variables, Java system properties, the shared credentials file, Amazon ECS container credentials, and EC2 instance profile credentials last. Developers must understand this order, because changing an IAM role's policy has no effect on an application's behavior if a higher-precedence credential source, such as environment variables, still exists on the instance. The policy type attached to the role, whether managed or inline, only becomes relevant once the SDK actually uses the role's credentials; it plays no role when a competing credential source intercepts the request earlier in the chain. Correct troubleshooting starts by checking every credential source ahead of the one the application is expected to use, not by assuming the newly applied policy is faulty.
Business scenario: At Bluecrest Alliance, a developer tightens an IAM role's policy to limit an EC2-based file-processing application to a single Amazon S3 bucket used for citizen benefit records, expecting this change to immediately restrict access. Because the EC2 instances still have AWS access keys stored as environment variables from an earlier deployment, the application keeps using those keys and retains access to every bucket. Removing the environment variables, or migrating fully to instance profile credentials, is required before the more restrictive IAM role can take effect.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-chap-configure.html

Option 1: The AWS credential provider looks for instance profile credentials last
Option 1 Explanation: Correct. The AWS SDK for Java uses a default credential provider chain when an application does not explicitly supply credentials. This chain checks sources in a fixed order: environment variables first, then Java system properties, then the shared credentials file, then Amazon ECS container credentials, and instance profile credentials last. Because access keys remain set as environment variables on the EC2 instances, the SDK finds and uses them before it reaches the instance profile credentials from the new IAM role. This is why the application still writes to all Amazon S3 buckets. Keyword tip: when environment variables and an instance role are both present, the credential chain always uses the environment variables first.
Option 2: An IAM inline policy is being used on the IAM role
Option 2 Explanation: Incorrect. An inline policy on the role does not explain this behavior either. When multiple policies apply to the same role, IAM combines them using a default deny plus explicit allow model. This combination produces the most restrictive effective permission; it does not create a bypass. The real issue is that the SDK never uses the instance profile credentials, because it finds the environment variable credentials first in the credential provider chain. Keyword tip: when multiple policies apply to one role, IAM always combines them into the most restrictive effective permission, never a bypass.
Option 3: The AWS CLI is corrupt and needs to be reinstalled
Option 3 Explanation: Incorrect. Nothing in the scenario indicates a corrupted installation. A well-documented explanation exists in the credential provider chain's order of precedence. Assuming software corruption without evidence is not a valid troubleshooting approach. Option 4: An IAM managed policy is being used on the IAM role
Option 4 Explanation: Incorrect. The scenario states the new IAM policy is more restrictive. Whether the role uses a managed policy or an inline policy does not matter here. The root cause is that the SDK uses environment variable credentials before it ever evaluates the role's credentials. The policy type attached to the role only matters once the SDK actually uses the role's credentials. Keyword tip: policy type (managed vs. inline) is not the answer when the credential provider chain never reaches the role's credentials.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question:
Following a spike in customer complaints about slow baggage-scan confirmations during peak boarding hours, an internal performance review at Silverlake Trust, a regional airline, examined the backend systems that process these events. The review focused on an AWS Lambda function that inserts scan records into an Amazon RDS for MySQL database, implemented as follows:
def handler(event, context):
     mysql = mysqlclient.connect()
    data = event['data']
    mysql.execute(f"INSERT INTO baggage_scans (scan_data)
VALUES ({data});")
    mysql.close()
    return
Monitoring data showed that the first invocation completes in 2 seconds, while the second invocation and every subsequent one still takes 1.9 seconds, almost no improvement despite AWS Lambda reusing the execution environment.  What should the development team do to reduce the Lambda function's execution time?
Correct Answer(s): Move the database connection logic outside of the handler function
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: initializing database connections, SDK clients, or other reusable resources outside the handler is a standard Lambda performance pattern that relies on execution context reuse.
Your Answer(s): Increase the Lambda function's allocated memory (RAM)
Overall Explanation:
This question tests understanding of the AWS Lambda execution context lifecycle and how to reuse resources across invocations to improve performance. Code placed inside the handler function runs on every single invocation, including expensive setup steps like opening a database connection. Code placed outside the handler function, at the global or module level, runs only once per execution environment and is reused by every warm invocation that follows. Increasing memory or upgrading downstream infrastructure only helps when profiling shows that compute power or server capacity is the actual limiting factor, which is not the case here, since the delay is caused by repeated connection setup and teardown.
A similar situation: Silverlake Trust's operations team could face the same pattern in a Lambda function that logs flight-crew check-in events to an RDS database, where each invocation opens a fresh database connection instead of reusing one from a previous warm invocation. By moving the connection setup outside the handler function, the team reduces per-invocation latency for high-frequency events like baggage scans or crew check-ins, without needing to change the database instance size or the programming language.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/running-lambda-code.html

Option 1: Upgrade the RDS MySQL instance type
Option 1 Explanation: Incorrect. Upgrading the RDS instance type gives the database server more compute and memory capacity. This scenario describes a delay caused by the client repeatedly opening a new connection, not by the database server lacking capacity. Keyword tip: separate database-side bottlenecks, such as query performance or instance sizing, from client-side bottlenecks, such as repeated connection setup.
Option 2: Increase the Lambda function's allocated memory (RAM)
Option 2 Explanation: Incorrect. Increasing the Lambda function's memory also increases its proportional CPU allocation. This change helps when the function is limited by CPU or memory. In this scenario, the delay comes from opening and closing a database connection on every call, not from insufficient compute power. Keyword tip: only choose a memory increase when the scenario points to a compute bottleneck, not when the bottleneck is connection management.
Option 3: Change the runtime to Node.js
Option 3 Explanation: Incorrect. Rewriting the function in a different runtime, such as Node.js, does not fix the real problem. The real problem is that the function creates and closes a new database connection on every invocation. This problem exists no matter which programming language the function uses. Keyword tip: when a question describes repeated expensive setup work inside the handler on every call, a runtime change is a distractor that ignores the root cause.
Option 4: Move the database connection logic outside of the handler function
Option 4 Explanation: Correct. The code creates the database connection inside the handler function. This forces Lambda to open a new MySQL connection and close it again on every single invocation. Opening a database connection is a slow operation. If the connection is created outside the handler function, in the global scope of the file, Lambda can reuse that same connection across multiple invocations that share the same execution environment. This removes the repeated connection setup cost from warm invocations and reduces execution time. Keyword tip: initializing database connections, SDK clients, or other reusable resources outside the handler is a standard Lambda performance pattern that relies on execution context reuse.

Use the AWS IAM service and let the application assume different roles depending on the type of user.

Question:
The development team at Orchardvale Agency, a book and media publisher that processes catalog update messages for its digital storefront, is using Amazon SQS FIFO queues to preserve the ordering of messages on a per-user_id basis. In addition to ordering, the team wants to ensure that duplicate messages are never delivered to consumers, since processing a duplicate would cause an application failure.
As the developer responsible for this implementation, which message parameter should you set to deduplicate messages?
Correct Answer(s): MessageDeduplicationId
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: when a scenario asks how to stop duplicate message delivery at the message level, MessageDeduplicationId is the parameter to configure.
Your Answer(s): ContentBasedDeduplication
Overall Explanation:
Amazon SQS FIFO queues provide two separate guarantees that solve two separate problems. MessageGroupId controls strict ordering within a group of related messages. MessageDeduplicationId, or the ContentBasedDeduplication queue setting, controls duplicate prevention so the same logical message is not delivered twice within the deduplication interval. ReceiveRequestAttemptId solves a third, unrelated problem: it deduplicates retried ReceiveMessage API calls, not the messages themselves. When a scenario asks specifically how to stop duplicate message delivery, choose MessageDeduplicationId if the producer supplies the token explicitly, or rely on ContentBasedDeduplication if you want Amazon SQS to derive the token automatically from the message body.
Business scenario: Orchardvale Agency publishes catalog updates for books and digital media through an event-driven pipeline. If a network retry causes the same catalog update message to be sent twice, duplicate processing could corrupt inventory counts or trigger duplicate customer notifications. By setting MessageDeduplicationId on each SendMessage call, the publishing team ensures that only one copy of each catalog update reaches the downstream consumer, while MessageGroupId keeps updates for the same title processed in the correct order.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/FIFO-queues.html

Option 1: ContentBasedDeduplication
Option 1 Explanation: Incorrect. ContentBasedDeduplication is not a message parameter. It is a queue-level setting. When enabled, Amazon SQS computes an SHA-256 hash of the message body and uses that hash as the deduplication ID automatically. The question asks for a parameter set on the message itself, so this queue-level setting does not match the requirement. Keyword tip: if the term describes a queue attribute rather than a value sent with each message, treat it as a distractor in questions asking for a message-level parameter.
Option 2: MessageDeduplicationId
Option 2 Explanation: Correct. MessageDeduplicationId is the token a producer sets on each SendMessage call to prevent duplicate messages from being delivered. If a message is sent successfully with a given deduplication ID, Amazon SQS accepts any later message with the same ID within the 5-minute deduplication interval, but does not deliver it to consumers. Option 3: ReceiveRequestAttemptId
Option 3 Explanation: Incorrect. ReceiveRequestAttemptId only works with FIFO queues, but it deduplicates ReceiveMessage API calls, not messages. A consumer uses this parameter to safely retry a failed ReceiveMessage request and get back the same batch of messages, even before the visibility timeout expires. This parameter does not prevent duplicate messages from being sent or delivered. Keyword tip: connect ReceiveRequestAttemptId to retrying a receive call, not to preventing duplicate message delivery.
Option 4: MessageGroupId
Option 4 Explanation: Incorrect. MessageGroupId groups related messages so Amazon SQS processes messages within the same group strictly in order. Messages in different groups can be processed out of order relative to each other. MessageGroupId controls ordering, not deduplication, so it does not meet the requirement of preventing duplicate delivery. Keyword tip: link MessageGroupId to ordering guarantees, not to duplicate prevention.

Question:
Confidential client case records at Fairmount Continental, a law firm, are currently stored in Amazon DynamoDB tables that rely on DynamoDB's default server-side encryption at rest. A new firm-wide data protection policy now requires that this sensitive data be encrypted before it is ever submitted to DynamoDB.
How can a developer meet this requirement?
Correct Answer(s): Use the DynamoDB Encryption Client to enable end-to-end protection using client-side encryption.
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: when a requirement says data must be encrypted before it leaves the application or before submission to a service, that phrase points to a client-side encryption library, such as the DynamoDB Encryption Client.

The UpdateTable operation can switch between these two key types, but UpdateTable never encrypts data before submission. AWS Certificate Manager is unrelated to encrypting DynamoDB item data, because ACM only manages TLS certificates for network transport. When a requirement states that data must be encrypted before it leaves the application, only a client-side encryption library, such as the DynamoDB Encryption Client, satisfies that requirement, because this library encrypts each item locally before the application calls the DynamoDB API.
In practice: A law firm like Fairmount Continental may need to guarantee that no unencrypted client case data ever leaves its application servers, even briefly, in order to satisfy strict client confidentiality agreements. By integrating the DynamoDB Encryption Client into its application code, Fairmount Continental encrypts sensitive fields locally before each write operation. As a result, the data that travels over the network and the data stored in DynamoDB are already protected end-to-end.

Question:

The consistency model then applies a multiplier to the read calculation: strongly consistent reads use 1 RCU per 4 KB unit per read, eventually consistent reads use half that many RCUs for the same throughput, and transactional reads use double the strongly consistent value. Writes follow a similar pattern, where standard writes use 1 WCU per 1 KB unit per write, and transactional writes use double that amount. The correct approach is always to round the item size first, then apply the correct multiplier based on the exact consistency or transaction type named in the scenario.
In practice: a cybersecurity consulting firm like Cobalt Labs often runs many parallel client engagements, each generating session data with predictable read and write patterns. Calculating RCU and WCU precisely before deployment lets the team provision DynamoDB tables that avoid throttling during audits or incident response work, while also avoiding overpaying for unused capacity. The item must round up to 5 KB, requiring 5 WCU per write, so 12 writes per second need 60 WCU. This question tests understanding of AWS KMS envelope encryption. AWS KMS limits direct cryptographic operations, such as Encrypt, Decrypt, and ReEncrypt, to payloads of 4 KB or smaller. When data is larger than 4 KB, the correct approach is to call GenerateDataKey. This API returns a plaintext data key and an encrypted copy of that same key. The application uses the plaintext data key with a client-side library to encrypt the actual payload, then discards the plaintext key and stores only the encrypted key alongside the ciphertext. GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlainText is reserved for cases where only the encrypted key is needed right away, while Encrypt and ReEncrypt only work on small payloads or on ciphertext that already exists.

Because each workpaper file regularly exceeds a few kilobytes, the developer calls GenerateDataKey to obtain a plaintext data key, encrypts the file locally with that key, and then stores the encrypted data key next to the encrypted file. This approach keeps large, sensitive financial records protected without exceeding the size limits of direct AWS KMS API calls.

DynamoDB provisioned capacity requires rounding the item size up to a fixed boundary before applying a per-second throughput formula: reads round up to the nearest 4 KB, and writes round up to the nearest 1 KB. The consistency model then applies a multiplier to the read calculation: strongly consistent reads use 1 RCU per 4 KB unit per read, eventually consistent reads use half that many RCUs for the same throughput, and transactional reads use double the strongly consistent value. Writes follow a similar pattern, where standard writes use 1 WCU per 1 KB unit per write, and transactional writes use double that amount. The correct approach is always to round the item size first, then apply the correct multiplier based on the exact consistency or transaction type named in the scenario.
In practice: a cybersecurity consulting firm like Cobalt Labs often runs many parallel client engagements, each generating session data with predictable read and write patterns. Calculating RCU and WCU precisely before deployment lets the team provision DynamoDB tables that avoid throttling during audits or incident response work, while also avoiding overpaying for unused capacity. DynamoDB rounds the 4.5 KB item size up to the nearest 4 KB boundary, giving 8 KB. A strongly consistent read of an 8 KB item needs 2 RCU per read, so 20 reads per second need 40 RCU. Eventually consistent reads need only half that number of RCUs for the same item size and throughput. The WCU value of 60 in this option is correct. The WCU value of 12 assumes the entire 4.5 KB item fits inside a single 1 KB write unit, which is incorrect. The item must round up to 5 KB, requiring 5 WCU per write, so 12 writes per second need 60 WCU. Keyword tip: WCU calculations round item size up to the next full 1 KB, so a 4.5 KB item always needs 5 WCU per write, not 1.

Question:
A security audit found that Keystone Collective's application on Amazon ECS uses long-lived access keys via the AWS SDK to call Amazon DynamoDB. Before moving to production, the developer must replace this with secure authentication.
How should the developer configure the application to securely authenticate to AWS services?
Correct Answer(s): Configure an ECS task IAM role for the application to use.
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: "task IAM role" is the standard secure-authentication pattern for ECS tasks calling AWS services like DynamoDB.

This question tests secure credential management for containerized workloads on Amazon ECS. The correct pattern is an ECS task IAM role, which attaches directly to the task definition and provides temporary, automatically rotated credentials scoped only to that task's containers. An ECS instance profile works differently: it grants permissions to the EC2 instance itself, so every task running on that instance shares the same permissions, which breaks the principle of least privilege. Static access keys, whether stored in environment variables or in a credentials file, are long-lived credentials that require manual rotation and increase the risk of exposure.
Consider this scenario: Keystone Collective's engineering team is migrating an ECS-based grading service that calls DynamoDB to store student progress data. Instead of packaging developer access keys into the container image, the team defines an ECS task IAM role scoped to only the DynamoDB tables the grading service needs. This way, if one microservice is compromised, the blast radius stays limited to that specific task's permissions, and CloudTrail logs show exactly which task made each API call.

Correct Answer(s): Redirect requests on cache misses to the S3 bucket nearest to the user's country. Create a Lambda@Edge function to redirect requests based on the value of the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header. Associate the Lambda@Edge function with the distribution's origin request event
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: origin request and origin response events are exclusive to Lambda@Edge and fire only on cache misses. Use this event whenever a question asks for logic that runs only when CloudFront must contact the origin.

Option 4: Use the AWS IAM service and let the application assume different roles depending on the type of user.
Option 4 Explanation: Correct. The application can assume a specific IAM role based on the user type. Each role has its own permission set. One role can allow access for registered users. A different role can allow access for guest users. This method does not require storing long-term credentials. This method also scales well as Highmoor Guild's user count grows. Keyword tip: when an application must switch permissions based on a runtime condition like user type, think 'assume different IAM roles.'
Option 5: Create a new IAM user for each user and grant access to the S3 objects.
Option 5 Explanation: Incorrect. Creating one IAM user for each of Highmoor Guild's 25,000 shoppers is not manageable. IAM enforces account-level quotas on the number of IAM users. This approach does not scale to a large user base. Keyword tip: when a scenario describes thousands of end users needing access, an IAM user per person is almost always the wrong, non-scalable distractor.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question: Vailmont National stores campaign bid values in DynamoDB. Multiple worker processes sometimes update the same campaign's bid value at nearly the same moment, and one worker's update is silently overwritten by another's. Which approach should developers implement to stop these updates from overwriting each other?
Correct Answer(s): Use conditional writes
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: look for phrases like "prevent overwriting concurrent updates" or "ensure updates are not lost" on a DynamoDB item — these phrases point to conditional writes with a condition expression.
Your Answer(s): Use conditional writes
Overall Explanation:
This question tests optimistic concurrency control in DynamoDB. By default, DynamoDB write operations are unconditional, so the last write always wins, even if that write overwrites a more recent change from another process. Conditional writes solve this problem by adding a condition expression that checks the item's current value before the write happens; if the value does not match what the writer expects, DynamoDB rejects the write instead of overwriting data. Atomic counters and batch operations solve different problems: atomic counters perform unconditional numeric increments, and batch operations group requests together purely for network efficiency, so neither one checks the item's prior state before writing.
Business scenario: Vailmont National's bidding engine runs many worker processes that each read a campaign's current bid value, calculate a new bid, and write the new bid back to DynamoDB. Without a condition expression, two workers that read the same starting bid value can both write their own updated bid, and the second write silently discards the first worker's change. By adding a condition expression that checks the bid value has not changed since the worker last read it, Vailmont National ensures that stale updates are rejected instead of applied, protecting the integrity of its real-time ad spend adjustments.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/WorkingWithItems.html#WorkingWithItems.ConditionalUpdate
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Expressions.ConditionExpressions.html

Option 1: Use concurrent writes
Option 1 Explanation: Incorrect. DynamoDB does not have a feature called "concurrent writes." Allowing writes to happen at the same time without any check is the actual cause of the problem in this scenario. Simultaneous unconditional writes can overwrite each other's changes without warning. The correct fix is to add a condition to the write, not to allow more concurrency. Keyword tip: treat any option that describes letting writes happen simultaneously without a check as a distractor in concurrency-control questions.
Option 2: Use atomic counters
Option 2 Explanation: Incorrect. Atomic counters use the UpdateItem operation to increase or decrease a numeric attribute. Atomic counters do this without checking the attribute's current value first. This makes atomic counters useful for values like a follower count or a like count, where losing an occasional increment is acceptable. Atomic counters do not protect against one bid update overwriting another bid update, because atomic counters never validate the item's prior state. Keyword tip: atomic counters solve unconditional numeric increments, not lost-update protection for arbitrary attribute values.
Option 3: Use conditional writes
Option 3 Explanation: Correct. DynamoDB write operations like PutItem and UpdateItem are unconditional by default. An unconditional write always overwrites the existing item, even if another process changed the item first. A conditional write adds a check before the write happens. The check compares the item's current value to an expected value, such as the bid value the worker originally read. If the current value does not match the expected value, DynamoDB rejects the write and returns an error. This rejection stops one worker's update from silently overwriting another worker's update. Keyword tip: look for phrases like "prevent overwriting concurrent updates" or "ensure updates are not lost" on a DynamoDB item — these phrases point to conditional writes with a condition expression.
Option 4: Use batch operations
Option 4 Explanation: Incorrect. Batch operations, such as BatchWriteItem, group several write requests into one network call. Batch operations reduce the number of round trips between the application and DynamoDB. Batch operations do not add any conditional check to the individual writes inside the batch. Because batch operations do not check the item's current state, batch operations cannot prevent one worker's update from overwriting another worker's update. Keyword tip: batch operations address network efficiency, not concurrency safety.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question: Kestrel Federation uses an AWS Step Functions state machine for sensor-data processing. During testing, a task state produced errors. A developer needs the state output to include both the original state input and the error message. Which coding practice should the developer use?
Correct Answer(s): Use ResultPath in a Catch statement to include the original input with the error.
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: when a scenario asks to merge or append an error onto the original input rather than overwrite it, think ResultPath.
Your Answer(s): Use ResultPath in a Catch statement to include the original input with the error.
Overall Explanation:
The Amazon States Language uses several fields to control how JSON data moves between states in a Step Functions workflow: InputPath, OutputPath, ResultPath, Parameters, and ResultSelector. InputPath selects part of the input before a state processes it. OutputPath selects part of the output before the workflow continues to the next state. ResultPath controls how a state's result, including an error captured by a Catch block, gets combined with the original input rather than replacing it. Retry statements, which use ErrorEquals, control re-execution attempts after a failure and play no role in shaping the combined output data.
Consider this scenario: Kestrel Federation runs a Step Functions workflow that ingests readings from thousands of smart city sensors. When a task state fails to parse a malformed sensor reading, the team needs the failed record and the error details stored together for review by the sensor maintenance crew. By adding a Catch statement with ResultPath set to append the error at a specific key, the original sensor payload stays intact in the output alongside the new error information, giving the maintenance crew everything they need in one record.
References:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/input-output-resultpath.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/tutorial-handling-error-conditions.html

https://cloudforall.com.br/cursos/aws-developer-associate-dva-c02-english/flashcards/
Option 1: Use ErrorEquals in a Retry statement to include the original input with the error.
Option 1 Explanation: Incorrect. ErrorEquals is used inside a Retry or Catch statement. ErrorEquals lists the specific error types that should trigger a retry or a catch action. ErrorEquals does not control how input data and error data are combined in the output. Keyword tip: ErrorEquals identifies which errors match a rule; it does not shape the output JSON.
Option 2: Use InputPath in a Catch statement to include the original input with the error.
Option 2 Explanation: Incorrect. InputPath selects which part of the original input is passed into a state for processing. InputPath does not run inside a Catch statement, and InputPath cannot merge error data with input data. Preserving both the original input and the error requires ResultPath, not InputPath. Keyword tip: InputPath narrows input before processing; ResultPath merges results or errors with input afterward.
Option 3: Use OutputPath in a Retry statement to include the original input with the error.
Option 3 Explanation: Incorrect. OutputPath selects which part of a state's output continues to the next state. OutputPath does not operate inside a Retry statement, and OutputPath cannot combine input data with error data. A Retry statement only controls re-execution attempts after a failure. Keyword tip: OutputPath filters output data; it has no connection to Retry logic.
Option 4: Use ResultPath in a Catch statement to include the original input with the error.
Option 4 Explanation: Correct. ResultPath controls where a state places its result inside the output JSON. When a Catch statement captures an error, ResultPath tells Step Functions to add the error information to the existing input instead of replacing the input. This keeps the original input and the error message together in the same output. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks to merge or append an error onto the original input rather than overwrite it, think ResultPath.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question:
Clearwater Logistics must guarantee that no unencrypted file is ever written to a specific Amazon S3 bucket. The company, a logistics and freight provider that stores sensitive shipment manifests and customs documentation in the clearwater-logistics-freight-docs bucket, has a written policy stating that all data placed in this bucket must be encrypted.
How can a Developer ensure compliance with this policy?
Correct Answer(s): Create an S3 bucket policy that denies any S3 Put request that does not include the x-amz-server-side-encryption header
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: a bucket policy Deny condition on the encryption header enforces encryption at upload time, rather than merely enabling it.
Your Answer(s): Enable Server-Side Encryption with Amazon S3-Managed Keys (SSE-S3) on the Amazon S3 bucket
Overall Explanation:
This question tests the difference between enabling encryption and enforcing encryption on Amazon S3. Default bucket encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) automatically encrypts an object when the upload request specifies no encryption method, but default encryption never rejects a request, so it cannot guarantee that every object is encrypted the way a strict policy requires. A bucket policy with an explicit Deny statement on the x-amz-server-side-encryption header is evaluated by Amazon S3 before the object is stored, so it can reject any PutObject request that omits the required header. Detective controls, such as a CloudWatch alarm, and access-control conditions, such as an x-amz-acl restriction, address different problems (after-the-fact notification and public access, respectively) and cannot substitute for a preventive encryption policy. When a scenario demands guaranteed compliance rather than a safety net, choose the option that denies the action outright based on a required condition.
A similar situation: Clearwater Logistics stores customs paperwork and shipment manifests for international freight in Amazon S3. Regulators require that this documentation always be encrypted at rest, with no exceptions. By attaching a bucket policy that denies any PutObject request missing the x-amz-server-side-encryption header, Clearwater Logistics guarantees that every file written by its shipping applications, third-party carriers, or automated pipelines is encrypted before Amazon S3 ever stores it, closing the compliance gap that a default-encryption setting alone would leave open.

https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-prevent-uploads-of-unencrypted-objects-to-amazon-s3/

https://cloudforall.com.br/cursos/aws-developer-associate-dva-c02-english/flashcards/
Option 1: Create a bucket policy that denies the S3 PutObject request when the attribute x-amz-acl has values public-read, public-read-write, or authenticated-read
Option 1 Explanation: Incorrect. This bucket policy statement blocks uploads that set public-facing access control list (ACL) permissions, such as public-read, public-read-write, or authenticated-read. This statement controls who can access an object. It does not check whether the object is encrypted. Keyword tip: x-amz-acl controls object access permissions, not encryption; do not confuse an access-control condition with an encryption condition.
Option 2: Enable Server-Side Encryption with Amazon S3-Managed Keys (SSE-S3) on the Amazon S3 bucket
Option 2 Explanation: Incorrect. Enabling SSE-S3 sets default encryption on the bucket. Default encryption means Amazon S3 automatically encrypts an object with S3-managed keys only when the upload request does not specify its own encryption method. Default encryption does not reject a request. It only fills in a fallback value when nothing else is specified, so it does not enforce the company's policy. Keyword tip: "default encryption" enables encryption, but it does not enforce or block anything.
Option 3: Create an S3 bucket policy that denies any S3 Put request that does not include the x-amz-server-side-encryption header
Option 3 Explanation: Correct. A bucket policy can include a Deny statement that triggers whenever a PutObject request does not include the x-amz-server-side-encryption header. Amazon S3 evaluates this policy before it stores the object. If the header is missing, Amazon S3 rejects the request outright, regardless of whether the intended encryption method was SSE-S3 (AES256) or SSE-KMS (aws:kms). This is the only option that actively blocks a noncompliant upload instead of only enabling encryption or reporting a violation afterward. Keyword tip: a bucket policy Deny condition on the encryption header enforces encryption at upload time, rather than merely enabling it.
Option 4: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that notifies an administrator if unencrypted objects are uploaded to the S3 bucket
Option 4 Explanation: Incorrect. A CloudWatch alarm is a detective control. A detective control reports a problem after the problem already happened. In this case, the alarm would only notify an administrator after an unencrypted object was already stored in the bucket. The policy requires that unencrypted data never be written to the bucket in the first place, so a detective control cannot satisfy this requirement. Keyword tip: alarms and notifications detect problems after the fact; they do not prevent problems from happening.

Test Paper: Exam 02 - AWS Certified Developer Associate DVA-C02
Question: Truenorth Dynamics runs a genomic sequencing pipeline on EC2 that produces many small metadata files, each about 1 KB, containing PII that must be encrypted. The files are stored on a proprietary NAS appliance with no native AWS KMS integration. What is the SAFEST way to encrypt the data using AWS KMS?
Correct Answer(s): Encrypt the data directly with a customer managed customer master key
Keyword Tip (Correct Answer): Keyword tip: when payload size is at or below 4 KB and the scenario requires full customer control over the key, encrypt the data directly with a customer managed customer master key.
Your Answer(s): Create a data encryption key from a customer master key and encrypt the data with the data encryption key
Overall Explanation:
AWS KMS supports two main encryption approaches: direct encryption with a customer master key, and envelope encryption with a data encryption key. Direct encryption works only for payloads up to 4 KB per operation, but it keeps the key material inside AWS KMS at all times, making it the safest option for small files. Envelope encryption is required for larger data volumes, but it forces the customer to manage the data encryption key's lifecycle outside of AWS KMS, which adds operational risk. The choice between an AWS managed customer master key and a customer managed customer master key depends on who needs control: AWS managed keys only exist for specific AWS service integrations, while customer managed keys give the customer full control and work with any storage system, including non-AWS systems.
Real-world example: A biotechnology research lab like Truenorth Dynamics generates thousands of small metadata files during genomic sequencing runs, each containing personally identifiable information about research participants. Because these files are stored on an in-house network-attached storage appliance with no native AWS integration, the lab cannot rely on an AWS managed customer master key. Encrypting each file directly with a customer managed customer master key lets the lab's security team retain full control over key policies and rotation while meeting strict data privacy requirements for research subject data.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/concepts.html

https://cloudforall.com.br/cursos/aws-developer-associate-dva-c02-english/flashcards/
Option 1: Encrypt the data directly with an AWS managed customer master key
Option 1 Explanation: Incorrect. An AWS managed customer master key is created and controlled by an AWS service, such as Amazon S3 or Amazon EBS, when that service needs to encrypt data on the customer's behalf. Truenorth Dynamics stores its files on a proprietary, non-AWS network-attached storage system, so no AWS service exists to request or manage an AWS managed customer master key for this data. Keyword tip: an AWS managed customer master key only appears when a supported AWS service creates it automatically; proprietary or unsupported storage systems cannot use one.
Option 2: Encrypt the data directly with a customer managed customer master key
Option 2 Explanation: Correct. A customer managed customer master key is created and fully controlled by the customer, including its key policy, IAM permissions, grants, rotation schedule, and deletion timeline. Each file is only 1 KB, which is within the 4 KB limit for direct encryption through the KMS Encrypt API, so no data encryption key is needed. Because the key material of a customer managed customer master key never leaves AWS KMS, this method gives the strongest security guarantee with the least operational complexity for small files. Keyword tip: when payload size is at or below 4 KB and the scenario requires full customer control over the key, encrypt the data directly with a customer managed customer master key.
Option 3: Create a data encryption key from a customer master key and encrypt the data with the customer master key
Option 3 Explanation: Incorrect. This option creates a data encryption key from a customer master key, but then encrypts the file with the customer master key instead of the data encryption key. Creating the data encryption key serves no purpose in this workflow, because the file is never encrypted with it. This wastes an extra API call to AWS KMS without adding any security benefit. Keyword tip: watch for options where a data encryption key is generated but the actual encryption step still uses the customer master key directly; this signals a broken envelope encryption workflow.
Option 4: Create a data encryption key from a customer master key and encrypt the data with the data encryption key
Option 4 Explanation: Incorrect. Creating a data encryption key from a customer master key and using the data encryption key to encrypt the data is the standard envelope encryption pattern. This pattern is designed for large files or high-volume encryption, because a customer master key can only encrypt up to 4 KB of data directly. Each file in this scenario is only 1 KB, so it fits within the direct encryption limit, and adding a separately managed data encryption key only increases operational risk without any benefit. Keyword tip: choose envelope encryption with a data encryption key only when data exceeds 4 KB or when the workload has high-volume or high-performance encryption needs.
